title: Stop CRED AutoPay for Card Bills and Flash Loans (2026)
metaDescription: Pause CRED AutoPay for card bills in the CRED app, find any UPI mandate behind it, and speak to the lender before stopping a CRED Flash loan mandate.
h1: How do you stop CRED AutoPay and the UPI mandates behind it?
summary: CRED lets you set a monthly AutoPay for credit card bills, and CRED says members can pause or stop it on the CRED app. CRED's UPI FAQ does not explain UPI mandates, so check any mandate in the UPI app or bank that approved it rather than assuming the CRED setting covers it. If the payment is a CRED Flash loan, speak to the lender first, because the loan agreement treats your bank being told to stop the mandate as an event of default.
keywords: stop CRED autopay credit card bill
stepsHeading: How to stop CRED AutoPay and check the UPI mandate

steps.name: Open the CRED app and find the AutoPay
steps.text: Open CRED and find the AutoPay setting against the credit card whose bill it pays. CRED's announcement does not give the exact menu path, so the label may differ by app version.

steps.name: Review the AutoPay details
steps.text: Check the monthly date, the bank account it draws from and the bill amount. CRED's announcement says AutoPay can pay a bill of up to ₹2 lakh a month, so confirm which bills it covers.

steps.name: Pause or stop it
steps.text: Pause or stop the AutoPay in the CRED app, which CRED says members can do. Keep the confirmation screen or take a screenshot.

steps.name: Watch for CRED's notices
steps.text: CRED says it notifies you when a bill is generated, before the payment is processed, and after it is completed. Use the pre-payment notice to confirm the change took effect before the next cycle.

steps.name: Check any UPI mandate in the approving app
steps.text: If you also approved a UPI mandate for a subscription or another bill, open the UPI app or bank app where it was approved and check its AutoPay or Mandates section. Do not assume that stopping the CRED setting has stopped it.

steps.name: Speak to the lender before stopping a Flash mandate
steps.text: A CRED Flash loan mandate belongs to the lender. Contact the lender before you stop anything, and do not close the linked bank account without its written consent.

steps.name: Use NPCI's help route if a mandate will not stop
steps.text: If you cannot find the mandate, try NPCI's UPI Help portal at upihelp.npci.org.in. For a debit you did not authorise, raise a complaint in the UPI app first.

sections.heading: CRED's own card-bill AutoPay
paragraphs: CRED's press release of 12 June 2026 describes AutoPay for credit card bills. You choose a date each month, and the bill, up to ₹2 lakh, is paid from your preferred bank account. CRED says it notifies you when a bill is generated, before the payment is processed, and after it is completed.

The release says members can pause or stop auto-pay on the CRED app, but it does not describe the screens. Follow the labels on your own version, and keep a record of the change so you can see on the next bill date whether it worked.

sections.heading: Is the card AutoPay also a UPI mandate?
paragraphs: The CRED pages I could read do not say whether a card-bill AutoPay creates a UPI mandate. CRED's UPI FAQ covers the roles of NPCI and the banks and the complaint process, but it does not mention mandates at all.
So if you see a UPI mandate in another app for a CRED-linked payment, deal with it in that app. If you cannot tell where a debit comes from, contact CRED support and ask which mechanism it uses.

sections.heading: CRED Flash loan mandates
paragraphs: The CRED Flash agreement says the lender may require an e-NACH or UPI mandate so that amounts due are collected automatically from your bank account. Clause 10.1.5 lists your instructing your bank to stop payment of the mandate as an event of default. Clause 12.1.6 says you must not close the linked bank account without the lender's prior written consent.
Opting out of the Autopay Service on the CRED app stops the automatic bill payments that service covers, but it does not change the loan. Speak to the lender before you change anything.

sections.heading: If a debit still goes through
paragraphs: CRED's UPI FAQ sets out the complaint sequence. The complaint starts with the app through which the payment was made, then goes to the PSP bank, your bank and NPCI, and finally to the Banking Ombudsman or the Ombudsman for Digital Complaints.
Keep screenshots of the debit, the cancellation and each complaint reference. Pre-debit notices and CRED's bill notifications are your best evidence of what was due and when.

sections.heading: Where Essara fits in
paragraphs: Essara works from a list you maintain. Add each subscription or mandate with its next debit date, and it shows the auto-debits due in the coming week and month, so you can check before the money leaves. It cannot pause a CRED setting, and it does not connect to CRED, your bank, your UPI app or SMS.

faqs.q: Can I pause AutoPay for credit card bills in CRED?
faqs.a: CRED's press release says members can pause or stop AutoPay on the CRED app. It does not give the exact label, so look for the setting against the card or bill in the app.

faqs.q: Does stopping CRED AutoPay also cancel the UPI mandate?
faqs.a: I could not confirm that from CRED's pages. Check the UPI app or bank app that approved any mandate rather than assuming it has stopped.

faqs.q: Can I stop a CRED Flash loan by switching off AutoPay?
faqs.a: Opting out of the Autopay Service stops the bill payments it covers, but the Flash agreement still applies. Its default clause covers your bank being told to stop the mandate, so speak to the lender before you act.

faqs.q: Will CRED tell me before it pays a bill?
faqs.a: Yes, according to CRED's press release. CRED says it notifies members when a bill is generated, before the payment is processed, and after it is completed.

faqs.q: Where do I complain about an unexpected UPI debit?
faqs.a: Start in the UPI app through which the payment was made. If that does not resolve it, the complaint moves to the PSP bank, your bank and NPCI, and then to the Banking Ombudsman or the Ombudsman for Digital Complaints.
